correctness.rationale: For every positive integer \(n\) and every unordered pair of letters, sufficiently long adjacent constant runs realize all \(n+1\) two-letter Parikh edge points. Their union has exactly \(3n\) elements. With ordered distinct integer weights and \(g=\gcd(\alpha,\beta)\), taking \(j=t\beta/g\) and \(i=t\alpha/g\) for \(1\le t\le\lfloor ng/\beta\rfloor\) yields two distinct occurring Parikh vectors of equal weight, for each \(t\); the collision sums are pairwise distinct. Hence the point-to-sum map loses at least \(\lfloor ng/\beta\rfloor\) classes. Repeated weights fail at \(n=1\). Each ordinary factor either starts before \(2^K<2n\) or contains at most one run boundary, giving \(P(n)\le5n+2\). Reading the bit length modulo three yields a four-state DFAO. Across the zero/one and one/two boundaries the natural weights realize every sum from \(0\) through \(2n\). The finite checker confirms 48 lengths and 343 valuations, but the infinite claims follow from the symbolic proof.

value.rationale: The published question asks whether some reweighting can preserve every abelian class count. Here the answer is negative within an explicit aperiodic ternary \(2\)-automatic word of linear ordinary factor complexity, with a quantified linear deficit for every injective integer valuation. Unlike a cheap superlinear-count pigeonhole argument, the obstruction is supplied by three structural Parikh-lattice edges. It identifies three as the least alphabet size and computes the exact natural additive complexity \(2n+1\), complementing the positive balanced-word theorem.
